FOREWORD This Indian Standard ( First Revision ) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Foodgrains and Foodgrain Industries Sectional Committee had been approved by the Food and Agriculture Division Council. Different types of barley are used for preparation of malt far brewing, distilling and other purposes. This grading of barley preparatory to malting is at present being done only by the maltsters. However, with the rapid expansion of breweries and alcoholic drinks industry, it was considered necessary to define and outline the characteristics on the basis of which barley should bt selected and evaluated for specific uses. This standard would be helpful in the orderly marketing of barley for industrial use. The limits for various characteristics stipulated in this standard have been arrived information and data collected from all over the country. at on the basis of

This standard was first published in 1973. It is being revised to update it in view of the latest technoIn the revised version requirements for hectolitre mass, specific logical developments in the country. gravity, yield of extract and starch percent have been included. Various terminology have also been modified to bring them in line with IS 2813 : 1970 ` Terminology for foodgrains (Jirst revision )`. A separate Indian Standard for malt ( IS 6895 : 1992 ), which is an adjunct also been published. In preparation restrictions

For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values ( revised )`. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

Type I barley shall be of plumper, heavier kernel type, aud Type II barley shall be of su~aller kernel size and high in nitrogen and enzynlic potentialities. 5 REQIJIREMEN'I`S 5.1 General Barley for malting purposes shall be either 2-rowed or 6-rowed. The kernels shall be with the white aleurone layers. The kernels shall be yellowishorstraw coloured with a fine, clean, uniform appearance. Barley for malting purposes shall be free from living insects and moulds and shall hejfrec from dead insects, insect fragments and rodent contamination visible to the eye (corrected, if necessary for abnormal vision) with the aid of a suitable niagnification (not exceeding x 10 ). Wheu cut transversely the kernels shall be maly and not steely. The barley shall not be smutty, garlicy, weevily, ergoty or bleached. 5.2 Size The size of barley kcruels shall be such that not less than 30 percent by I\\ass of kernels are retained on a sieve of aperture 2.S mm; not less than 80 percent by mass are rctaincd ou a sieve of apcrlure 2.2 mm. The proportion of kcrncls passing through a 2.2 mnl aperture sieve shall not cxcecd 2 percent by ulass.

For the purpose of this standard, the following definitions shall apply. 3.1 Sound Barley Kernels of barley remaining after removal of foreign nlatler (set 3.2) and damaged keruels (&c 3.4). 3.2 Foreign Matter Includes inorganic aud organic matter. The inorganic matter includes sand, gravel, dirt, pebbles, stones, glass and metallic piec.es, lumps of earth, clay and mud. Organic matter includes husk, chaff, straw, weed seeds and other inedible grains. Paddy is considered as foreign matter in conmodities other than paddy. 3.3 Other Foodgrains Foodgrains other thau the grain under consideration. 3.4 Damaged Kernels Kernels or pieces of keruels that are sprouted or internally damaged as a result of heal, nloisturr, wcatheror microbes.

A-3 PROCEDIJRE Fill the cylinder with toluene at about 20�C and weigh. Then empty the cylinder. Add about 20 g of grains and toluene up lo three quarters level. Close the cylinder with the stopper and slowly turn lo and fro. Fill the cylinder conlpletely with toluenc and put the stopper in such a way that no air bubble remains; wipe the cylinder dry and weigh. Finally pour the contents of the cylinder into a large fluted filter preferably of kieselguhr containing paper. The filtered toluene can be rc-used several limes. NOTEThe quickest method is to use a direct reading
analytical balance of the Mettler type, which does not need weighing to accuracy more than approximately 0.01 g. It is not necessary to usea thermostat, as iflhe temperature is not exactly 20�C the result can be accordingly rectified.

Mark

The use of the Standard Mark is governed by the provisions of the Br~eau Q/" Ztuliurl Stmtlurtls Act, lY86 and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder. The Standard Mark on products covered by an Indian Standard conveys the assurance that they have been produced to comply with the requirements of that standard under a well defined system of inspection, testing and quality control which is devised and supervised by RIS and operated by the producer. Standard marked products are also continuously checked by BIS for conformity to that standard as a further safeguard. Details of conditions under which a licence for the use of the Standard Mark may be granted to manufacturers or producers may be obtained from the Bureau of Indian Standards.

Bareaa of Iodiaa Staadardr BIS ir-a statutory institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote harmonious development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods and attending to connected matters in the country. Copyright BIS has the copyright of all its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced m any form without the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course of implementing the standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. Enquiries relating to copyright be addressed to the Director ( Publications ), BIS. Review of Indian Standards Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are any reviewed periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, !t is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of `BIS Handbook' and `Standards Monthly Additions'.
